column3: Escher staircase. Three panels touching corner to corner down a diagonal are three treads of an endless, impossible staircase (Escher's Ascending and Descending, Penrose stairs), drawn in an axonometric engraving style; the black voids between the panels are the drop the stairs step over. A slinky (rainbow coloured, the owner's frog colours, or polished brass) walks down forever with real slinky physics: it arcs end over end from tread to tread, the top coils falling over into the bottom, coils bunching and spreading as a travelling wave; when it leaves the bottom tread it re-enters at the top, Penrose-impossibly. The time belongs to the stairs: hours on the top tread, minutes on the bottom, the middle tread for something that ticks (or a better split of your own), as numerals inlaid, carved or built into the treads in the same projection (design a stone-mason or engraved letterform for it). Minute turn: the slinky lands on the changing digit, coils around it and compresses it, and as it springs off it leaves the new digit behind (the coil wrapping into the new numeral and unwinding). Hour: the staircase does an Escher trick (gravity flips, the stairs rotate into Relativity, or a parade of slinkies descends). The corner-to-corner shape is the idea: use the voids.

Toy train layout. Eight panels round an empty centre are a 192x192 square picture frame, and the frame is a model railway running all the way round (top-down or a tin-toy 3/4 view): a station on the top side, a tunnel through a hill at one corner, a bridge over a pond, a level crossing with a barrier and waiting cars, trees, little houses with lit windows by night, signals that change. The hollow middle is part of the joke: the train runs round a real hole. The time rides the train: a steam loco driven by the owner's frog (bold, 16+ px, flat rainbow bands, white-rimmed round glasses, smile) pulls four wagons, each carrying a big numeral as its cargo (wooden letters, stacked crates, a lit sign board, or the numeral shaped from the cargo itself: logs, coal, toys); design a toy-shop numeral that is chunky and carved. Most of the minute the train stands at the station across the top with the digits upright and readable, alive with steam, smoke rings, passengers, the station clock's seconds, the crossing's traffic, ducks on the pond. Minute turn: the changing digit's wagon uncouples and is shunted away or craned off, and the new cargo arrives on a sidetrack and couples on with a bump (0.8-3 s, physical, eased). Hour: the full train does a grand lap of the frame (through the tunnel, over the bridge, whistle and steam, digits riding along and still readable) and returns to the station. Use the ring: the train actually goes round.

Video wall. Nine panels, 3 by 3, are a stacked wall of nine old CRT television sets (a Nam June Paik video sculpture, or a TV-shop window at night): each panel is one TV, so the panel grid becomes the sets' cabinets and bezels (wood-grain and bakelite, knobs, rounded tube corners), and each tube has its own life: scanlines, phosphor glow, vignette, a slight barrel curve, its own colour cast and quirks (one rolls, one has ghosting, one is a bit green). The time is broadcast across the wall as one giant picture split over the nine tubes, broken by the bezels (a 70s station-ident or broadcast-graphics numeral, designed for 192x192 with the bezel gaps in mind), while individual sets drift into their own channels and back (a test card, static snow, the frog weather presenter, an aquarium, a cartoon). Always alive: scan crawl, flicker, interference bars, a V-hold roll. Minute turn: a channel change on the sets carrying the changing digit: real CRT effects (vertical roll, static burst, the picture collapsing to a line and a dot on switch-off and blooming back on warm-up) and the new digit tunes in. Hour: all nine sets break into different channels for a show (the frog's hour broadcast, a countdown), then snap back into one synchronised picture. The 3x3 grid of panels is the idea: one wall, nine screens.

Tiny city at night. Nine panels are a 192x192 top-down living miniature city (Mini Motorways / SimCity): the time is the city plan itself, the four numerals drawn by its road network and parks or by blocks of lit buildings, readable across the room as a map. Cars are moving lights with real traffic behaviour (white headlights one way, red tail lights the other, lanes, signals, queues at junctions, a bus stopping, a train on a viaduct, boats on a river, a plane's blinking lights crossing). Day and night follow the real time: by day rooftops, trees and parks; by dusk the windows switch on block by block; at night the roads become rivers of light and the numerals glow like a city seen from a plane (the wow). Minute turn: roadworks: the changing digit's streets are coned off, traffic reroutes, and the new numeral's streets are paved segment by segment by tiny trucks and light up as cars flood in (0.8-3 s, smooth). Hour: something city-wide and joyful (stadium fireworks, a parade of lights along the avenues, a blackout that comes back block by block in the hour's shape), with the time readable throughout. Use the size: real streets, real traffic, a whole city.

Elevator building. Six panels (128x192 portrait) are the cutaway of a ten-storey building, floors 0 to 9 from the ground up, with a lobby, a roof with a water tower and a sky that follows the real time. It is a doll's-house cross-section: lit rooms with little residents (the frog cooking, a cat on a sofa, a party, someone asleep), lights going on and off by the time of day. Four elevator shafts run up through it, one per digit (hour tens, hour units, minute tens, minute units): each car parks at the floor of its digit, so the time is read as the four cars' floors against big floor numbers painted on the shaft walls: not digits anymore (urwerk-like), but the scale must read clearly. Real elevator motion: jerk-limited acceleration and levelling, cables and counterweights moving opposite, a car light, passengers inside, doors opening and closing. Always alive: residents move, a light flicks on, the minute-units car's passengers come and go, a floor-indicator needle in the lobby swings. Minute turn: the changing car rides from its old floor to the new one (9 to 0 is an express drop, with the counterweight shooting up past it), doors open with a ding. Hour: all four cars move together, a party on the roof, fireworks over the water tower. The tall shape is the building.

Pop-up book. The 128x64 board is an open pop-up storybook seen from a little above the spine: the two-page spread is the board's shape. The numerals are paper engineering standing up from the pages in real 3D (V-folds, layered paper planes, tabs, paper shadows, lit by a warm reading lamp), with illustrated scenery around them (a storybook world of your choosing: castle, forest, sea, night sky) and paper characters on pull-tabs and wheels that slide, wave and spin (the frog on a tab). Design a storybook numeral: cut-paper letterforms with paper thickness, folds and printed texture. Always alive: tabs slide, a paper moon swings on its thread, a volvelle wheel turns with the seconds, paper sways in a draught. Minute turn: a page turns with a real 3D curl over the spine, the old pop-up folding flat as its page lifts and the new one unfolding and standing up as the page lands (pop-up geometry driven by the page angle: the fold-flat and rise is the wow). Hour: the whole book closes and opens again at a new chapter (the hour as the chapter title) with a bigger pop-up (a dragon, a castle) that rises. Keep the time readable through both.

Birthday cake in the dark. A 128x128 close-up of a birthday cake in a dark room, lit only by its candles. The time is four numeral candles (wax candles moulded as numbers, the kind sold for birthdays: design a numeral-candle font with wax shading, a wick, slow drips, a pastel or glitter finish) standing on a cake with piped icing, sprinkles and frosting, arranged as a composition (not a plain row of four: two tiers, hours on top, or your own). The flames are the wow on black GOB: real flame simulation (flicker, sway in a draught, a soot wisp, a glow that lights the wax from inside, the icing and the faces around the table). Always alive. Minute turn: the owner's frog (bold, 16+ px, flat rainbow bands, white-rimmed round glasses, smile, leaning in from the side, cheeks puffing) blows out the changing candle (the flame bends, gutters and smokes), a hand swaps in the new numeral candle and a match relights it with a flare. Hour: the lights come up for the party (confetti, a banner, all flames flare), then the room goes dark again. Unlit candles must still read in the neighbours' light.

Rube Goldberg machine. A 256x64 workshop wall with a long chain-reaction contraption running across the banner (marbles on ramps, dominoes, a swinging boot, a seesaw, a bucket filling, a candle burning a string, a mouse wheel, a fan blowing a sail, a toaster, a spring, the frog on a seesaw). The time is the machine's output: four big numerals each shown by a different mechanism (a drum of painted number cards turned by a pawl, flipping wooden slats, a sign that pops up, stacked blocks, a pegboard), all in hand-painted signwriter numerals on wood designed for this grid. Always alive: the machine idles in small loops (a marble recirculates on a lift, a pendulum ticks the seconds, a hamster runs, a cuckoo bobs). Minute turn: the chain reaction fires (start it early so it lands on the minute): real physics, rolling marbles, falling dominoes, a lever, travelling along the banner to the changing digit's mechanism, which changes it in 0.8-3 s. Hour: the whole machine fires end to end, ending in something joyful (the frog launched from a cannon, confetti, a flag going up). The long banner is the track the reaction travels.

Brick breaker. A 64x192 tall arcade screen playing Breakout / Arkanoid, glowing on black: the walls of bricks ARE the time (hours as a brick formation near the top, minutes below), built from bricks of different materials (glass bricks with a highlight, silver that take two hits, gold that can't break), in a brick font designed for this grid and the brick size you choose. A paddle piloted by the owner's frog plays forever by AI: the ball streaks with a comet trail, bounces with real reflection off the curved paddle and walls, and long flights use the tall screen; it only ever hits background bricks and power-up capsules (which respawn), never the time. Minute turn: the ball (or a laser or multiball power-up) smashes exactly the bricks the old digit has and the new one lacks, bricks shattering into particles, and new bricks fly in or are laid for the ones the new digit needs, landing with a bounce; the time is never wrong (missing bricks are fine, extra ones are not). Hour: multiball frenzy, a ROUND banner, every brick flashes, the warp gate opens. Arcade glow.

Claw machine. A 64x128 claw crane cabinet seen from the front: a neon marquee at the top, the glass window with the gantry and a three-pronged claw on a cable, a heap of plush prizes at the bottom, the prize chute. The time is plush: four numeral-shaped stuffed toys (felt numbers with stitched seams, button eyes and little faces: numberfolk) sitting on top of the heap in view, among other plushies (frogs, ducks, bears). The claw is always alive: the gantry glides, the cable swings as a real pendulum, the claw opens and closes, it fumbles a prize (the classic weak grip: things slip). Minute turn: the claw (already on its way in the last seconds) comes down, grabs the old numeral plush (it squashes in the grip), drops it down the chute, then fishes the new numeral out of the heap and sets it in place, all physical: swinging cable, plush squish, a bounce on landing. Hour: jackpot: chasing lights, prizes rain into the chute, the frog plush wins. Glass reflections and the marquee glow are the finish.

Latte art. A 64x64 top-down view of a cup of coffee on a saucer: the round cup fills most of the panel, and the corners are the café table (a spoon, a sugar cube, a crumb). The time is latte art: the numerals are poured in milk foam on the crema (a barista's pour font: thick-to-thin, the rosetta wiggle, white microfoam with a soft edge against brown crema), designed for this small grid. Always alive: the pattern drifts on a slow swirl, foam bubbles pop, steam wisps curl over the surface, a highlight slides on the cup rim, the crema shimmers. Minute turn: a spoon dips in and stirs the changing digit away (a real 2D advection field with a vortex from the spoon, the foam smearing into a spiral), then the milk jug's stream pours the new numeral with a barista's wiggle and pull-through. Hour: the whole cup is stirred into a vortex and a fresh pour draws the hour as a grand rosetta (or a frog face etched with a toothpick), then the time again. Smooth fluid is the wow; keep it deterministic (advect from a minute-keyed state in closed form or a short warmup).

Frost on a window. A 64x64 window pane on a winter night: through the glass, out-of-focus city lights (warm bokeh) and falling snow in parallax; on the glass, frost. The time is ice: the numerals are frost crystals growing on the pane (fern frost and dendrites, sparkling where light catches their facets), each digit's skeleton seeding the growth; design frost letterforms whose strokes are bands of feathery branches. A good trick: compute an arrival-time field per digit once (when each pixel freezes, grown out from the strokes with branching noise), then growth is just a threshold that rises with time, closed form and smooth. Always alive: snow drifts outside, crystals sparkle and creep at their tips, a melt droplet occasionally runs down. Minute turn: a warm breath fogs the changing digit and melts it (condensation bloom, droplets running), and the new digit crystallises outward along its strokes, branches racing like time-lapse frost. Hour: the whole pane fogs, a finger draws a little frog in the fog, then frost reclaims the glass and the time. Cold blue-white ice on deep night blue against warm bokeh.

Cat's cradle. Two hands (the owner's frog's, green with round fingertip pads, or a child's pair from each side) play cat's cradle in a spotlight on black, a loop of glowing string (yarn or neon thread) stretched between their fingers. The time is the string: the figure between the fingers forms the numerals, every stroke a taut straight segment between finger points, with crossings (string-figure letterforms; the four digits as one figure, or a figure per pair of hands, or hours and minutes on two strings). Real string physics: the loop is a rope pinned to fingertips, it sags, vibrates when plucked, trembles as the hands breathe. Minute turn: a transfer move: fingers pinch crossings and pull through, the figure collapses and re-forms into the new numeral (length conserved, never a wrong number in between), hands sliding and twisting: the dexterity is the show. Hour: the string flips into a classic figure (Jacob's ladder, the Eiffel tower, cat's whiskers) for the hour, then back. Glowing string on black is the light; the hands are the characters.

Pool hall. The 128x64 board is a pool table seen from above (2:1, a real table's shape): green baize in a pool of light from a low lamp, wooden rails with diamond sights, six pockets. The time is the balls: numbered pool balls (solids and stripes, with their numbers and a specular highlight, rolling with visible spin: the number and stripe turning on the sphere in real 3D) arranged at rest into the numerals (ball formations as letterforms: design how a numeral reads in 10-20 balls on this grid, maybe with chalk-drawn guide lines or a rack). Always alive: the frog (bold, 16+ px, seen from above, cue in hand) walks round the table lining up shots, chalks the cue, the lamp sways a touch, a cue ball idles. Minute turn: a trick shot: the cue ball breaks the changing digit's formation, balls scatter with real elastic collisions and cushion bounces and roll to rest exactly in the new numeral (make it a deterministic physics solve, or steer subtly so it looks real). Hour: a full break, balls drop into the pockets counting the hour, then the rack is set again. The physics is the wow.

Night beach. A 192x64 panorama of a shoreline at night under the moon: dry sand, the wet mirror-shiny band, waves rolling in. The time is written in the sand: four numerals traced with a stick (grooves with raised lips, lit by the moon at a raking angle; a hand-drawn-in-sand script designed for this grid). The waves are the wow: real wave run-up and backwash (a height field along the beach, foam lines and lace, the sheen of the receding film), and the water glows with bioluminescent plankton (blue sparks where it breaks and where feet touch it). Always alive: waves every few seconds, crabs scuttle, stars, the moon's glitter path; the palette follows the real time (sunset, day, night). Minute turn: a bigger wave runs up over the changing digit, which softens and smooths away as the water recedes, and the owner's frog (bold, 16+ px, flat rainbow bands, white-rimmed round glasses, smile) walks along and writes the new digit stroke by stroke with its stick, leaving footprints. Hour: a high wave washes the whole line in glowing blue and the hour is written in plankton light before the sand version returns. Use the panorama: the beach runs the length of it.

Bullet hell. Five panels in a plus are the arena of a danmaku shoot 'em up. A boss fills the centre panel (an ornate rotating core: rings of turrets, a glowing eye, petals), firing hypnotic bullet patterns: spirals, flowers, rings, curving streams, hundreds of glowing orbs with additive glow on smooth sub-pixel paths. In each of the four arms the bullets settle into one numeral, written in a curtain of slowly orbiting bullets (a bullet font: dotted strokes of round orbs, bigger at joints and ends, upright in every arm). The frog's ship (bold, 12+ px, recognisably the rainbow frog in round glasses) weaves through the patterns grazing bullets, its focused shot chipping at the boss. Minute turn: the boss fires a spell card at the changing digit's arm: the old bullet-numeral is cancelled (bullets turn into score items that stream to the player) and a new stream blooms from the core and flows along curved paths into the new numeral. Hour: a phase change: a SPELL CARD banner, a screen-filling pattern, the frog bombs, the core's rings reassemble, the time readable throughout. The plus is the arena: four lanes round a core.
